name: Revenue growth
formula: Revenue(t) / Revenue(t-1) - 1
why_it_matters: How fast sales are growing; the first sign of market share gains or losses.

name: EBITDA growth
formula: EBITDA(t) / EBITDA(t-1) - 1
why_it_matters: Whether operating profit grows faster or slower than sales.

name: Net profit growth (reported)
formula: Profit for the year(t) / Profit for the year(t-1) - 1
why_it_matters: Growth in the bottom line as reported; distorted in years with exceptional items.

name: Underlying profit growth
formula: Profit before exceptional items and tax(t) / same(t-1) - 1
why_it_matters: Profit growth with one-off gains and losses removed.

name: Gross margin
formula: (Revenue - materials - stock purchases - change in inventories) / Revenue
why_it_matters: Share of sales left after raw material costs; paint inputs are crude-oil linked, so this shows cost pressure and pricing power.

name: EBITDA
formula: Revenue - materials - stock purchases - change in inventories - employee costs - other expenses
why_it_matters: Operating profit before depreciation, interest, tax, other income and one-offs.

name: EBITDA margin
formula: EBITDA / Revenue
why_it_matters: The core measure of operating efficiency; the main way analysts compare paint companies.

name: Net profit margin (reported)
formula: Profit for the year / Revenue
why_it_matters: Bottom-line profitability as reported; includes exceptional items and other income.

name: Underlying profit margin
formula: Profit before exceptional items and tax / Revenue
why_it_matters: Pre-tax profitability without one-offs; comparable across companies and years.

name: Return on equity (reported)
formula: Profit attributable to owners / average equity attributable to owners (start and end of year)
why_it_matters: Profit earned for shareholders on the money they have in the business.

name: Return on capital employed
formula: (Profit before exceptional items and tax + finance costs) / average (total equity + borrowings)
why_it_matters: Profit on all long-term capital (equity and debt); includes treasury income from cash held.

name: Total borrowings
formula: Non-current borrowings + current borrowings (excluding lease liabilities)
why_it_matters: How much the company owes lenders.

name: Cash and liquid investments
formula: Cash and cash equivalents + other bank balances + current investments
why_it_matters: Money available quickly.

name: Net cash (negative = net debt)
formula: Cash and liquid investments - total borrowings
why_it_matters: Positive means more cash than debt; a cushion for price wars, capex or dividends.

name: Debt to equity
formula: Total borrowings / total equity
why_it_matters: Leverage; low for all three companies.

name: Free cash flow
formula: Net cash from operating activities - capital expenditure
why_it_matters: Cash left after investing in the business; funds dividends and acquisitions.

name: Capex intensity
formula: Capital expenditure / Revenue
why_it_matters: How heavily the company is investing in capacity.

name: Cash conversion (OCF / net profit)
formula: Net cash from operating activities / Profit for the year
why_it_matters: Do reported profits turn into cash? Below 1 can mean cash stuck in working capital; distorted when profit includes one-off gains.

name: Cash conversion (OCF / EBITDA)
formula: Net cash from operating activities / EBITDA
why_it_matters: Same question, before tax and one-offs, so comparable across years and companies (tax paid keeps it below 1).

name: Receivable days
formula: Trade receivables / Revenue x 365 (year-end balance)
why_it_matters: How long dealers take to pay; longer credit is a way to win dealers.

name: Inventory days
formula: Inventories / cost of goods sold x 365 (year-end balance)
why_it_matters: How long stock sits before being sold. Cost of goods sold = materials + stock purchases + change in inventories.

name: Payable days
formula: Trade payables / cost of goods sold x 365 (year-end balance)
why_it_matters: How long the company takes to pay suppliers.

name: Cash conversion cycle
formula: Receivable days + inventory days - payable days
why_it_matters: Days of sales tied up in working capital; lower is better.
